Status: accepted for this research implementation. Production activation and recursive self improvement remain outside demonstrated scope.

## Decision

RuVLLM owns mechanical model inspection, bounded patching, reversible checkpoint changes and evidence packaging. An external authority owns promotion and activation. A proposer cannot turn its own benchmark or signature into production permission.

The implementation separates three experimental claims:

1. Self repair corrects a specific observed failure mechanism.
2. Self optimization improves previously unseen tasks under an unchanged evaluation protocol.
3. Recursive self improvement makes the optimizer measurably better at producing subsequent improvements at equal compute.

Each claim requires separate evidence. Reproducing an existing published edit does not establish an independently discovered repair or recursive improvement.

## Checkable invariants

1. The source checkpoint remains unchanged. Candidate and rollback outputs use new paths.
2. Every changed tensor and value must fit an explicit policy. Protected ranges, changed value count and absolute or relative delta bounds are checked before publication.
3. A candidate is bound to its original checkpoint, patch, policy and generation identities.
4. Paired comparisons use the same prompts, decoding settings, output budgets and serving precision. Completion and delivered correctness are separate measurements.
5. Development data select candidates. Release evidence is retained, including regressions and failed attempts.
6. Evaluation validates model, runtime, protocol and topology identities before aggregation. Mixed generations are rejected.
7. Qualification, authorization and observed activation are distinct records. This repository exposes no production activation tool.
8. Rollback restores original bytes, verified by full digest and byte comparison.
9. A deployment generation change requires new cache identity across every serving peer. Distributed pee

The Rust engine and scoped plugin implement inspection, bounded edits, rollback, receipt validation and RVF integrity. The Python runners implement actual inference comparison and independent saved output scoring. The coding adapter and surgical edit are evaluated separately.

Core Memory authority was tested in a separate local reference workspace using proposer, evaluator and readback credentials under one operator. This repository does not include that service or claim independently operated certification. The measured 0.8B quality gate failed and did not authorize production activation.

# ADR 012: MetaHarness bounded weight experiment runner

Status: accepted for the CPU research integration, 2026-11-03.

## Context and outcome

RuVLLM already enforces tensor allowlists, protected ranges, delta bounds and
exact rollback. The native `evaluate` operation validates receipts; it does not
perform inference. Repeating this lifecycle manually makes it easy to compare
different baselines, lose failed candidates, or mistake an efficiency gain for
an accuracy improvement. We need a repeatable experiment controller that keeps
those native guarantees and explicitly records the origin of evaluation claims.

The actors are a trusted local operator, a proposer (possibly Claude), and an
external evaluator. The operator alone selects the executable, roots, policies,
timeouts and maximum candidate count. A proposer supplies a plan and cannot
change these controls. An evaluator supplies measurements bound to checkpoints,
patches, runtime, protocol and suite identities. No actor receives production
activation authority from this integration.

# Experiment protocol

Objective: reduce the cost of narrow coding and tool use requests routed from Claude Code while preserving correctness. An open base and small adapter support distribution without redistributing Claude weights.

## Inputs and outputs

1. Model preparation takes the pinned Apache 2.0 Qwen3.5 4B repository and produces a hashed MLX 4 bit model with group size 64. The original BF16 download remains intact.
2. Training takes only the original training and validation traces and produces PEFT adapters at steps 32, 64, and 96. Only 16 MLP output projections receive rank 8 updates. The remaining base parameters stay frozen. Training is BF16 on an A100; deployment uses the separately measured quantized base.
3. Development evaluation takes each checkpoint and the same frozen prompts, temperature zero, seed 20261102, disabled thinking, and 768 output tokens. It produces raw responses, executable scores, token counts, completion status, and wall time.
4. Selection requires at least one additional correct case without group regression, or equal correctness with at least 10% fewer output tokens. Two consecutive nonimprovements stop checkpoint evaluation. No failed trial is removed.
5. Release evaluation takes the selected checkpoint once. The synthetic release set and 164 task HumanEval suite measure beh

## Controls

The controller allows at most four evaluation iterations, three training checkpoints, four hours total wall time, and one hour per stage. A file lock prevents duplicate workers. A stop request terminates the active local process group and cancels its cloud training job. Failed stages require explicit inspection and resume. Cloud jobs also have provider timeouts independent of the local controller.

The USD 200 cloud cap uses integer micro USD reservations before dispatch. The full timeout plus one billing minute is reserved. Reservations remain charged against the local cap even if a job fails or its actual bill is lower. Network ambiguity never triggers automatic redispatch. Billing estimates use the live hardware API. Actual invoices remain provider records.

Cloud inputs are original synthetic data and public model weights. Checkpoints live in a private bucket mounted by the provider. Cloud workers receive no user access token, local repositories, or private conversations. No public model upload occurs automatically.

Evaluation code runs under a macOS Seatbelt profil

## Known limitations

The pilot has few independent template families, one decoding seed, and only 8 synthetic coding tasks per split. Small pass count improvements can be statistical noise. HumanEval measures short Python functions and may have appeared in base pretraining. Real repository editing, long context, multilingual programming, sustained tool error recovery, concurrent serving, and long running sessions need separate evaluation.

Quantization and adapter training are separate interventions. Compare the quantized baseline with the adapter on the same quantized base. Report the BF16 baseline separately. A100 and Mac timings use different hardware and runtimes and are not direct latency comparisons.

Anthropic's gateway documentation does not support non Claude models. CCR compatibility is verified locally and may change with client updates. The deployment profile supports text only and 16384 total tokens. Use a stronger router fallback for other requests.

**Tamper-proof hashing and signing for every RVF segment -- SHA-3 digests, Ed25519 signatures, and lineage witness chains.**

```toml
rvf-crypto = "0.1"
```

Every operation on an RVF file gets recorded in a cryptographic witness chain. `rvf-crypto` provides the primitives that make this possible: SHA-3 (SHAKE-256) content hashing for segment identity, Ed25519 digital signatures for provenance, and lineage verification functions that ensure no record in the chain has been altered. If you are building tools that read, write, or transform `.rvf` files, this crate handles all the cryptography so you do not have to.

| | rvf-crypto | Manual hashing + signing | No integrity checks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Segment identity** | SHAKE-256-256 content-addressable IDs | Roll your own digest scheme | Rely on filenames |
| **Provenance** | Ed25519

# RuVLLM **Change a model. Prove it. Keep the original.** RuVLLM trains and edits small adapters for open language models, then measures each one against the unchanged base on the same tasks, under a rule written before the results. Every decision to keep or reject an adapter is backed by every raw answer, a paired significance test and a local re-score. The original weights restore byte for byte. ## Why RuVLLM

| Benefit | How it works |
| :--- | :--- |
| 🔒 **Rules locked first** | Tasks, expected answers, generation settings and the keep rule are frozen into a SHA-256-pinned bundle before any model output exists. |
| ⚖️ **Paired, per-task statistics** | Base and candidate answer identical tasks on the same GPU. Gains and losses are tested with an exact McNemar test, not compared as two averages. |
| 🔍 **Regressions stay visible** | Results break down by tool family and by case, with a failure taxonomy, so a gain in one place can't hide a loss in another. |
| ♻️ **Byte-exact restore** | The Rust engine edits a copy inside an explicit policy and proves restoration with matching source and restored hashes. |
| 💸 **Cheap, capped GPU runs** | Four spending limits, an independent destroy timer and confirmed cleanup on every rental. |
| 🧰 **Works where you work** | npm CLI, Claude Code plugins over MCP, a Ruflo-compatible server and an OpenAI-compatible local API on Apple Silicon. |

# anndists

This crate provides distances computations used in some related crates [hnsw_rs](https://crates.io/crates/hnsw_rs), [annembed](https://crates.io/crates/annembed) and [coreset](https://github.com/jean-pierreBoth/coreset)

All distances implement the trait **Distance**:

```rust
pub trait Distance<T: Send + Sync> {  
    fn eval(&self, va: &[T], vb: &[T]) -> f32;
}
```

## Functionalities

The crate provides:

* usual distances as L1, L2, Cosine, Jaccard, Hamming for vectors of standard numeric types, Levenshtein distance on u16.

* Hellinger distance and Jeffreys divergence between probability distributions (f32 and f64). It must be noted that the Jeffreys divergence
(a symetrized Kullback-Leibler divergence) do not satisfy the triangle inequality. (Neither Cosine distance !).

* Jensen-Shannon distance between probability distributions (f32 and f64). It is defined as the **square root** of the Jensen-Shannon divergence and is a bounded metric. See [Nielsen F. in Entropy 2019, 21(5), 485](https://doi.org/10.3390/e21050485).

* A Trait to enable the user to implement its ow

### Simd

It is recommanded to use the compile flag **target-cpu=native** to activate dynamic cpu feature detection, for example
adding **RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native** in your environment.

* The simd provided by the simdeez crate is accessible with the feature "simdeez_f" for x86_64 or aarch64 processors.
Compile with **cargo build --release --features "simdeez_f"**.

* It is also possible to experiment with std::simd. Compiling with the feature stdsimd
(**cargo build --release --features "stdsimd"**), activates the  portable_simd feature on rust nightly. **This requires nightly compiler**.
Only the Hamming distance with the u32x16 and u64x8 types and DistL1,DistL2 and DistDot on f32*16 are provided for now.

The speed is illustated in the [hnsw_rs](https://crates.io/crates/hnsw_rs), [annembed](https://crates.io/crates/annembed) crates

Rust implementation of the CRC-32-Castagnoli algorithm with hardware acceleration where possible.

    * Only available on rust version >= 1.80.0 or nightly

All other processors utilize a software fallback.

Computing dot-products, similarity measures, and distances between low- and high-dimensional vectors is ubiquitous in Machine Learning, Scientific Computing, Geo-Spatial Analysis, and Information Retrieval.
These algorithms generally have linear complexity in time, constant or linear complexity in space, and are data-parallel.
In other words, it is easily parallelizable and vectorizable and often available in packages like BLAS (level 1) and LAPACK, as well as higher-level `numpy` and `scipy` Python libraries.
Ironically, even with decades of evolution in compilers and numerical computing, [most libraries can be 3-200x slower than hardware potential][benchmarks] even on the most popular hardware, like 64-bit x86 and Arm CPUs.
Moreover, most lack mixed-precision support, which is crucial for modern AI!
The rare few that support minimal mixed precision, run only on one platform, and are vendor-locked, by companies like Intel and Nvidia.
SimSIMD provides an alternative.

The package is intended to replace the usage of `numpy.inner`, `numpy.dot`, and `scipy.spatial.distance`.
Aside from drastic performance improvements, SimSIMD significantly improves accuracy in mixed precision setups.
NumPy and SciPy, processing `i8`, `u8` or `f16` vectors, will use the same types for accumulators, while SimSIMD can combine `i8` enumeration, `i16` multiplication, and `i32` accumulation to avoid overflows entirely.

## Algorithms & Design Decisions 📚

In general there are a few principles that SimSIMD follows:

- Avoid loop unrolling.
- Never allocate memory.
- Never throw exceptions or set `errno`.
- Keep all function arguments the size of the pointer.
- Avoid returning from public interfaces, use out-arguments instead.
- Don't over-optimize for old CPUs and single- and double-precision floating-point numbers.
- Prioritize mixed-precision and integer operations, and new ISA extensions.
- Prefer saturated arithmetic and avoid overflows.

Possibly, in the future:

- Best effort computation silencing `NaN` components in low-precision inputs. 
- Detect overflows and report the distance with a "signaling" `NaN`.

Last, but not the least - don't build unless there is a demand for it.
So if you have a specific use-case, please open an issue or a pull request, and ideally, bring in more users with similar needs.

### Cosine Similarity, Reciprocal Square Root, and Newton-Raphson Iteration

The cosine similarity is the most common and straightforward metric used in machine learning and information retrieval.
Interestingly, there are multiple ways to shoot yourself in the foot when computing it.
The cosine similarity is the inverse of the cosine distance, which is the cosine of the angle between two vectors.

```math
\text{CosineSimilarity}(a, b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{\|a\| \cdot \|b\|}
```


```python
    elif ab == 0: result = 1                              # Division by zero error in SciPy
```

The Fused-Multiply-Add (FMA) operation is a single operation that combines element-wise multiplication and addition with different scaling factors.
The Weighted Sum is it's simplified variant without element-wise multiplication.

```math
\text{FMA}_i(A, B, C, \alpha, \beta) = \alpha \cdot A_i \cdot B_i + \beta \cdot C_i
```

```math
\text{WSum}_i(A, B, \alpha, \beta) = \alpha \cdot A_i + \beta \cdot B_i
```

SimSIMD exposes all kernels for all backends, and you can select the most advanced one for the current CPU without relying on built-in dispatch mechanisms.
That's handy for testing and benchmarking, but also in case you want to dispatch a very specific kernel for a very specific CPU, bypassing SimSIMD assignment logic.

## 1. What is ruvllm

RuVLLM's tagline is "Change a model. Prove it. Keep the original." It trains and edits small adapters for open language models, then measures each one against the unchanged base model. Both run on the same tasks, under a keep/reject rule written before any results exist. The original weights restore byte for byte.

The repo mixes npm and Python, with a Rust native engine (`native/`, built with cargo). It is indexed as 2 components and 510 public symbols.

## 4. How it works

The README describes a four-step lifecycle:

1. **Freeze.** Pin the model revision, task panel, generation settings and keep rule. Tasks and expected answers go into a SHA-256-pinned bundle before any model output exists. The panel is 256 cases: 8 tool families × 24, plus arithmetic as a retained-capability anchor. `experiments/model-improvement/prepare.py` creates the bundle.
2. **Change a copy.** Train a LoRA adapter or apply a bounded weight edit. The original file is never modified.
3. **Measure in pairs.** Run base and candidate on identical tasks and keep every raw answer. Score with the frozen scorer.
4. **Decide and restore.** Apply the preregistered rule, then verify that the original restores byte for byte (matching source and restored hashes).

Deployment needs separate approval. The measurement protocol is written up in ADR 016, and the Vast.ai host adapter in ADR 017.

sections.h: Getting better is easy to fake
sections.q: Why is improving an AI model so easy to get wrong?
sections.text: You tweak an AI model, try it a few times, and it seems smarter. Can you trust that feeling? Imagine coaching a friend for a spelling bee. After a week, they ace the practice words you picked. Are they really better? Maybe those words were easy. Maybe they got worse at math while they practiced spelling. Tuning an AI model has the same trap. People choose the test questions after seeing the results. They compare two averages and keep whatever looks good. It is like grading your own homework and being very pleased with the A. A big gain in one place can quietly hide a loss somewhere else. There is a second pain. Many people edit the model itself. If the edit turns out bad, the good original is gone, and there is no way back. Nobody enjoys that moment.

sections.h: A safe way to improve a model, and show your work
sections.text: RuVLLM lets you improve an open AI model without gambling on it. Think of a clothing store fitting room: try the new outfit on, and the original stays on its hanger. It trains a small add-on. That is a tiny set of extra numbers that sits on top of the model and nudges how it behaves. The original model is never touched. Then it runs the plain model and the model with the add-on on identical questions. Every answer is saved. Nothing is thrown away. In the repo's own recorded runs, one add-on was kept and a second one was rejected. That is the system working as intended.

sections.h: The clever move: write the rules before the game
sections.text: Two ideas make the proof hard to fudge. Picture calling your shot in pool before you hit the ball. First, the questions, the right answers and the keep-or-reject rule are locked before the model answers anything. Nobody can shift the goalposts after seeing a score. Second, the old and new versions answer the very same questions. For each question, you ask who got it right. You count how many the add-on fixed and how many it broke. The repo's own second try shows why this matters. The add-on fixed every tool mistake. But it forgot how to add, and lost 16 math answers. The locked rule said math must not get worse, so it was rejected. Nobody had to argue about it. Call your shot before you take it, and the scoreboard cannot be talked into agreeing with you.

sections.h: Freeze, change a copy, measure in pairs, decide
sections.q: How does it work, step by step?
sections.text: The workflow has four steps. Each one is checked by saved evidence. Freeze: the model version, the task list, the answer settings and the keep rule are sealed in a bundle. The bundle gets a SHA-256 fingerprint (a short code that changes if even one character changes). Prepared tasks cover eight families of coding-tool use, with 24 cases each. Arithmetic is a separate check that the model's general skills have not slipped. Change a copy: there are two ways. A LoRA adapter (a small add-on trained while the base model stays frozen) is the main one. The included add-on, coding-4b, has about 1.5 million trainable numbers. The other way is a direct weight edit. A Rust program changes specific values inside a copy, within a strict policy. Measure in pairs: both versions run on the same graphics card (the chip AI models run on). Gains and losses are checked with an exact McNemar test. That test looks only at questions where the two versions disagree. On the held-out panel, coding-4b went from 149 to 176 of 192 tool passes, with 40 gains and 13 losses. Arithmetic went from 62 to 64. Decide and restore: the frozen rule says keep or reject. The Rust engine then proves the original comes back by matching fingerprints. Rented graphics cards run under four spending limits and a separate self-destruct timer, so a forgotten rental cannot eat your wallet. Recorded runs cost between $0.27 and $0.91 each. A job counts as done only when a re-score on your own machine matches.
